html:
You roll into work at 9:30 on Wednesday the 4th of November, 2037.

Overnight, the follow-ups from yesterday's meetings have gone out. The CRM is up to date. Proposals are drafted, reports are built, and every goal the firm has shows exactly how far it is from target.

You open your laptop to the firm's harness. There isn't much to see. Your goal for the quarter and how you're tracking: 41 of 50 returns signed off, two weeks to go. Then your work for the day:

  • 10am: coffee with JPC Automotive. The agents have set up a meeting with your biggest client to go through their audit. They're nervous, so they need to hear it in person. You're given talking points.
  • Sign the Hendersons' return. Everything's checked. Click approve and your signature goes on it.
  • 2pm: Mia wants to open a second store. The agents have modelled three scenarios. Walk her through them and help her pick.
  • Afternoon: a new offer for local tradies. Workshop it with the team. The agents will build whatever you land on.

You close the laptop and head to the cafe.

This is the future of work. With perfect context and always-on AI models, everything else was done before you arrived. What's left is the work that needs a human: being in the room, putting your name on it, and the strategising pushing the firm forward. The firm serves 3x as many clients as it did 5 years ago, and none of your work is repetitive.

Why I Think This Is Coming

For many, this state is the natural conclusion of where AI is currently.

I think AGI, at least for the work most companies do, is already here. The models are no longer the blocker. If they have a clear goal and full context, and they can do most white-collar work. What's usually missing is the systems around the model.

A company can be distilled down in its simplest form to a series of loops. Every company has a goal, ideally a number and a date: say $10M/year revenue in five years. It is then possible to work backwards to the highest leverage yearly and quarterly goals, then finally monthly, weekly and daily tasks. Each loop feeds the one above it.

Agents thrive at running loops, assuming they have a strict definition of done. A goal with a number and a date ("3 discovery calls booked by 16 Oct") can be checked automatically, and once it can be checked, an agent can keep working at it until it's done. Every company goal can therefore be broken down into mostly agent work, with some human pieces along the way.

Context is the other half. The agents in 2037 know what was said in yesterday's meetings, what's in every email, and how nervous the client is about their audit. Today that context is scattered across inboxes, calendars and people's heads, and getting it to the agents is one of the biggest unsolved challenges in AI.

None of this is a new idea. HR tools have tried to run companies on measurable goals for decades. They failed because humans had to fill them in, and nobody fills in the form. Agents don't have that problem.

This is already happening, mostly inside AI-native companies. We're a team of six at Hourglass, and a lot of my week already runs like the 2037 firm. The future I'm describing is here for many, it's just waiting to be diffused.

What Work Is Fundamentally Human

If agents can do most things, the human work comes down to a few key pieces:

  • Relationships. People trust people. Agents can prepare every number, but a nervous client, a big negotiation or a hard conversation still needs someone in the room who cares how it lands.
  • Accountability. Someone's name has to be on the work. When a decision goes wrong, a client wants a person who owns it, not a log file.
  • Taste and judgement. Knowing when something technically works but isn't right. Saying no to the feature, the deal or the re-brand, because you know what the company stands for on an emotional level.
  • Creativity and strategy. Deciding where the company goes next: the new offer, the market nobody's serving, the idea that sounds crazy. Agents can model every option, but inventing them and choosing which is still human.

Companies Already Doing This

Spawn is the best proof I've seen that part of this is already here. Their article on this went viral last week: a team of ten shipped 77,000 changes in 30 days, alongside a fleet of agents that each own part of the product.

"Most companies run big human teams that use AI, and we run a small human team alongside a big team of agents."

Even there, the humans didn't disappear. By October they stated that the only thing left waiting on people was decisions of taste.

Polsia goes further. Its pitch is "AI that runs your company while you sleep": an AI CEO wakes up every night, decides what to work on and does it. The company raised $30M at a $250M valuation this year.

However, Polsia tries to get to the 2037 state by removing humans entirely. They have a roughly 50% monthly customer churn rate, and I'd argue it's because you can't actually achieve longterm value selling to humans without the human work to get there.

How We're Getting There

At Hourglass we're building toward this in two parts. Neither would have worked a year ago without Opus 5.5.

The first is Hourglass OS: one place for our North Star, the goals under it and the outcomes under those, each with one owner. Every outcome is a number and a date. Goals rank themselves by how far they are from target, so priority gets computed by an algorithm instead of argued. Everyone arrives at work knowing the top 3 needle moving things they can do that day.

The second is what I've started calling the work factory. The big idea in AI coding right now is the software factory: agents turn specs into software. The work factory applies the same idea to the rest of the business, where the goal is the spec. We have 10+ agents always on, picking up actions from meetings, emails and Slack. What comes back to me is a short board of decisions, not a to-do list, with agents carrying out the grunt work.

It's far from perfect. In 2037 the system runs itself. Today, people still have to run it: keeping it alive, fixing what breaks, and catching where a number lies. However, considering how far LLMs have progressed in the past year, it won't be long before it's near-perfect.

Sharpen the Axe

Every founder and operator right now should be figuring out how to make their goals and company context AI-readable.

A lot of this starts with strategy: what is the company actually trying to do, as a number and a date? Break that into discrete chunks of work. Then start building the systems that do those chunks, one at a time, so each one compounds on the last.

You don't need to build the 2037 firm today. You just need to know what it looks like, and take the next step towards it to stay AI-native.

If you want the playbooks and systems I use to run Hourglass, they're open source → thehourglass.ai/finlay.
